clue.text: Pretty shy hugging me at rear of school

indicators.note: To hug somebody is to get your arms right round them, so the word in front closes over the letters named next.

parts.note: somebody shy about being looked at is coy
the setter's own 'me' goes in as its two letters, unchanged

indicators.note: The rear of a word is the letter it ends on, and that single letter is all this takes.

parts.note: the letter at the back of 'school'

explanation.surface: A bashful admirer clinging to the speaker round the back of the school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty shy' reads as one phrase, a fairly timid person, and the split falls between the two words: the first is the definition and the second is material.
explanation.definitionFit: Comely is the old-fashioned adjective for good-looking, so 'Pretty' swaps straight in wherever it stands.

clue.text: Budgie perhaps free in big cedar

indicators.note: Something set free is no longer held where it was put, and letters let loose like that can settle in any order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A pet bird let loose among the branches of a big cedar tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the setter's flag for definition by example: a budgerigar is one of these rather than the word for all of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A budgie is one instance of the class, a bird kept in a cage, so the definition names the whole group by a single member.

clue.text: Swell breakfast item

definitions.meaning: the verb for growing fast and wide, the way demand or a town does
one of the things in the pan beside the bacon in a British cooked breakfast

explanation.surface: Somebody calling a breakfast dish absolutely swell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' reads as the American adjective for excellent, praising whatever is on the plate, and the sense wanted is the verb for growing rapidly.
explanation.definitionFit: To mushroom is to swell — costs mushroom, meaning they balloon — and the noun is a fry-up staple.

clue.text: An idiot picked up sponge

indicators.note: Picking a thing up lifts it, and in a down clue lifting means reading the letters back up the column from bottom to top.

parts.note: the indefinite article, taken as its own single letter
a fool is an idiot

explanation.surface: An idiot bending down to pick a sponge up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An idiot' looks like the person doing the picking up, and it is the material, article included — 'An' is as much a part of the letters as the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried gourd sold as a bath sponge, so 'sponge' names it by the job it does in the bathroom.

clue.text: Get over arch, and one may make a bolt for it

definitions.text: one may make a bolt for it

parts.note: to get over a road or a river is to cross it
a bow is an arch: a bow window bulges out in the same curve

explanation.surface: Somebody climbing over an arch, where anyone might suddenly run for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a bolt for it' is the idiom for dashing away, and the bolt the setter means is the short heavy arrow the weapon shoots.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbow fires bolts, so the description is literal: the bolt is its ammunition rather than an escape.

clue.text: Brazen volte-face about poem, 'Polecat'

parts.note: re means about or concerning, the way a memo heading is written
verse is poetry, so a poem is a piece of it
the domesticated form of the polecat, which is why the setter puts the word in quotes rather than claiming it outright

explanation.surface: A shameless U-turn, and a poem called 'Polecat'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like an instruction to turn something round, and the volte-face beside it encourages that reading; it is only the two-letter word for concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverse ferret is Fleet Street slang for a newspaper suddenly and shamelessly changing its line, which is a brazen volte-face.

clue.text: People searching for these here but they lack concentration

definitions.note: Neither half is a plain synonym: the first points at the answer through the people hunting for it, and the second through a property the chemist's sense can have.
definitions.meaning: 'here' is the puzzle in front of you, and everybody filling in a grid is hunting for these
the chemist's sense, reached sideways through a property: a weak mixture is one with very little dissolved in it

explanation.surface: A complaint that the people hunting for something here cannot keep their minds on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: Chemistry supplies the second sense: liquid with something dissolved in it, and a dilute one has hardly any concentration in it at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Solutions are what a solver hunts for in a grid, and in chemistry the same word names a dissolved mixture, weak when the concentration is low.

clue.text: Reach the top of chest

definitions.meaning: the climber's verb: you do this to a hill when you come over its crest
the front of the torso, from collarbone down to ribs

explanation.surface: Climbing up to the top of a chest.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together as one instruction about a piece of furniture, and 'of' is the join: a runner breasts the tape and a walker breasts the hill.
explanation.definitionFit: To breast a slope is to reach its top, and the breast is the chest, so one word covers the climb and the body.

clue.text: Hardy folk lived here in primarily wild county

indicators.note: What comes primarily is what comes first, so only the opening letter of the word after it is taken.

parts.note: the letter 'wild' starts with
Essex is an English county, on the coast just east of London

explanation.surface: Tough country people once living in a rough and untamed county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' reads as an adjective for those tough folk, and it is Thomas Hardy, who set his novels in a half-invented corner of south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Wessex is the old Saxon kingdom Hardy revived as the setting of his novels, so 'here' points at that fictional south-west.

clue.text: Relish oxygen brought by sudden wind

indicators.note: The wind is what carries the other piece along, so whatever it brings is set down after it.

parts.note: a gust is a sudden rush of wind
o is the chemist's symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A sudden squall of wind blowing fresh air about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' looks like the verb — to relish a challenge — and the noun is wanted, the zest somebody does a thing with.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is the relish you do something with: 'ate with gusto' and 'ate with relish' ask for the same appetite.

clue.text: Old Parliamentary radicals who told it to you straight?

definitions.meaning: the movement that pressed the Civil War Parliament of the 1640s for equal rights and a vote for ordinary men

definitions.text: who told it to you straight
definitions.meaning: to level with somebody is to tell them the truth with nothing dressed up, and these are the people who do it

explanation.surface: Politicians of the past who never dodged a question.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second half as a joke rather than a dictionary sense, and the capital P sells the first half as history.
explanation.definitionFit: The Levellers were English radicals of the 1640s, and a leveller is also anyone who levels with you — plain speaking, no flattery.

clue.text: Hello again, rector: still not made a bishop?

parts.note: a rector who is still only a rector has been one for ages
a bishop is given a see, the district he presides over, so a clergyman passed over has none

explanation.surface: Running into a long-serving rector and asking whether he has been passed over for promotion again.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop's see is his diocese — the word survives in the Holy See — so a priest never promoted to one genuinely has no see to his name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is what you say to somebody you have not run into for ages, which is a greeting on meeting again rather than a first hello.

clue.text: Deal-maker in pub, one taking a profit

parts.note: the bar is where a pub serves its drinks, and stands for the place itself
somebody who gains is a gainer — a share that rises is one of the day's gainers

explanation.surface: A dealmaker propping up a pub bar, out to take his cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it is putting one thing inside another, which is what that word usually does in a clue; here it only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargainer is somebody who haggles over terms until a deal is struck, so 'Deal-maker' names them by what the haggling produces.

clue.text: A brief experience of discrimination

definitions.meaning: a short sample of something — a few days of it, enough to know what it is like
the older sense of the word: the judgement that tells the good from the shoddy

explanation.surface: A short spell of being discriminated against.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discrimination' pulls hard towards prejudice, because that is the only sense in daily use now, and the setter wants the faculty of telling fine from cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: A taste of something is a brief sample of it, and a person of taste discriminates between good and bad — two senses of the noun.

clue.text: Lower tier seats filled first for this film?

parts.note: the surface picture is an auditorium filling from the bottom up, the cheap seats downstairs going before the rest
the question mark says a title is wanted, so what you must name is the state the upper tier has been left in

explanation.surface: An usher reporting that the cheap seats downstairs always go before any of the others.
explanation.walkthrough: Room at the Top is the 1959 British film of John Braine's novel about a young man clawing his way up, and the phrase itself means scope for promotion.
explanation.definitionFit: If the lower tiers fill first the space left is literally up above, and that phrase is the title of the 1959 film.

clue.text: Ideas for a reform mentioned earlier

indicators.note: To reform a thing is to shape it again, so the letters just before it are given a new arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Proposals for a reform that somebody has already brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' reads as the thing the ideas are for, part of the same noun phrase, and it is the instruction acting on the words in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Aforesaid is the legal drafter's adjective for something already named in the document, which is exactly what was mentioned earlier.

clue.text: New American widescreen system

indicators.note: Making a thing new is making it over from what was already there, and the letters that follow are made over the same way.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A brand-new American way of showing films on a very wide screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New American' reads as one phrase about a modern invention, so nothing looks like an instruction; the process really was American, which is the setter's wink.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinerama was the 1950s process that threw three projectors onto one deeply curved screen, so 'widescreen system' describes it plainly.

clue.text: Cook breakfast, including coffee, getting insincere praise?

indicators.note: To include a thing is to have it inside you, so the coffee named next sits within the word before it.

parts.note: to fry is how a breakfast gets cooked, bacon and eggs in the pan
a latte is a coffee, espresso lengthened with hot milk

explanation.surface: Cooking a fry-up with a coffee alongside, and being buttered up for it.
explanation.walkthrough: A fry-up is the British cooked breakfast, which is why 'Cook breakfast' points at one particular verb rather than at a whole menu.
explanation.definitionFit: Flattery is praise laid on to please rather than because it is true, so the question mark marks it as the sly half of the clue.

clue.text: In isle grey tomb crumbling, typically romantic

indicators.note: A tomb crumbling falls into pieces that no longer sit where they were, and the letters come apart the same way.

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A grey tomb falling apart on an island, which somebody finds terribly romantic.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphens in the enumeration are the giveaway that a set phrase is coming rather than a word, and the definition wants a plot rather than a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the standard romance storyline, and it is used as an adjective — a boy-meets-girl story — which is what the hyphens signal.

clue.text: Spoke of what one has in each arms

definitions.meaning: one of the bars running from a wheel's hub out to its rim

definitions.text: what one has in each arms
definitions.meaning: the shorter of the two bones in the forearm, and everybody has one on each side

explanation.surface: Somebody talking about what a person is carrying in each arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoke' looks like the past tense of speak, which is the only way the surface sentence works, and the setter wants the noun from a wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A radius is a spoke, the line from a wheel's centre to its rim, and it is also the forearm bone paired with the ulna in each arm.

clue.text: Shrub and vegetable penetrated by decay

indicators.note: To penetrate a thing is to go right into it, so the letters named afterwards sit inside the word before.

parts.note: a pea is a vegetable
rot is what decay does to fallen fruit

explanation.surface: A shrub and a vegetable going rotten in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like it is joining two things in a list, so the shrub and the vegetable seem to be a pair; only one of them is being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A protea is a South African flowering shrub, the king protea being that country's national flower, so 'Shrub' names its kind plainly.

clue.text: Have no argument with an Athenian amputee

indicators.note: An amputee has had a limb taken off, so the word beside it loses the letter at its end.

parts.note: the article itself, dropped in as one letter
an Athenian is a Greek, Athens being the capital of Greece

explanation.surface: Getting on peaceably with an Athenian who has lost a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have no argument with' reads as one phrase and the 'with' is only joinery, so the definition stops a word earlier than the ear expects.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is to have no argument: once you agree there is nothing left to dispute, so the definition states it from the negative side.

clue.text: Missile landing in sniper's lair: this tightest of squeaks?

indicators.note: A thing that lands in a place comes to rest inside it, so the missile's letters end up within the lair's.

parts.note: a sniper shoots from a nest, the hidden position he settles into
an arrow is a missile in the older sense, anything shot or thrown
surface only: it completes the idiom for a close escape, the sort you only just get through

explanation.surface: A missile coming down on a sniper's hideout, about as close a call as anyone could have.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeaks' sounds like mice in the lair; the idiom being aimed at is a narrow squeak, a hair's-breadth escape.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrowest is tightest of margins: a narrow squeak and a tight squeeze both mean getting through with almost nothing to spare.

clue.text: Many times relent, though not at first

indicators.note: This takes away the letter standing at the front, so the word has to start one place later than it did.

parts.note: to soften is to relent: you soften your line when you give ground

explanation.surface: Somebody who gives way plenty of times, just never straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Though not at first' reads as a concession about timing — he relents in the end — and it is an instruction about the front of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means on many occasions, so 'Many times' is the plain adverbial swap: it happens often, it happens many times.

clue.text: On journey, train isn't moving

indicators.note: Letters that are moving are not staying where they were put, so the ones just named shift into a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A train that has stopped somewhere and is going nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't moving' reads as one phrase about a stationary train, and the two words belong to different jobs: one is material and the other is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods in transit are on their way from one place to another, so 'On journey' is the same state in plainer words.

clue.text: Track down a very tiny amount

definitions.meaning: to follow something to where it is now, as police do with a missing person
the barely detectable quantity a chemist reports, too small to measure properly

explanation.surface: Hunting down the last tiny scrap of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions run together as one sentence about a search, and 'down' belongs to the first of them rather than to the amount.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace somebody is to track them down, and a trace of a substance is the smallest detectable amount of it — one word, verb and noun.

clue.text: Kubrick briefly portrayed Scottish patron

indicators.note: Asking for a name briefly asks for its everyday short form, so the back end of it is left off.

parts.note: the film director Kubrick's first name was Stanley
to portray somebody is to draw them, and this is the past tense

explanation.surface: Kubrick giving a short performance as Scotland's patron saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kubrick briefly portrayed' reads as one clause about a director playing a part, and 'portrayed' has been borrowed from that clause for the second half of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland, whose diagonal cross flies as the saltire on the Scottish flag.

clue.text: Not simple, so restive

parts.note: un- is the prefix that negates a word, as in unfair or unkind
an easy task is a simple one

explanation.surface: Something that is not straightforward and so leaves everybody restless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not simple' reads as one phrase meaning complicated, and it splits into a prefix and the word that prefix negates.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive means restless and hard to settle, which is how somebody uneasy feels — the word is about disquiet, not about difficulty.
